Some were struck in gold, some in silver, others in copper and other metals. Museums, antiquities collections, and private collections contain coins struck in southern Arabia, some in gold, some in silver, and others in copper. Some small coins carry the name of the king during whose reign they were struck. Some, however, are ancient and go back to the period before the Common Era. Jawad Ali also argues, same source, p. 206, that the people of the Hijaz used not only Roman and Sasanian coins—dinars, dirhams, and daniq—but also Yemeni and Ethiopian coins in the pre-Islamic period and in early Islam before Islamic coins with Arabic inscriptions were struck. Meccans in particular traded with Yemen, Iraq, and Syria and therefore used many different currencies. Conditions in their own country were not favorable for minting coins locally.↩︎

One revealing example shows that private ownership of livestock was widespread. al-Aghani, vol. 16, p. 95, tells a story about Hatim al-Ta’i, who died forty-five years before the Hijra. Banu Lam wanted to compete with Hatim at the market of al-Hira by making a wager involving his horse. When Iyas ibn Qabisa al-Ta’i heard of this, he feared Hatim might be defeated and lose the wager, so he gathered his people from Banu Hayya and urged them to support their cousin Hatim. One man said: “I have one hundred black camels and one hundred reddish camels.” Another stood and said: “I have ten stallions, each with a fully armed rider.” Hassan ibn Jabala al-Khayr said: “You know that my father died and left great wealth. I will provide all the wine, meat, and food for as long as they remain at the market of al-Hira.” Iyas then said: “I will give as much as all of you together.” The story continues that Hatim’s cousin Wahm ibn Amr said: “No. This is my property, numbering nine hundred camels. Take it from him until the camels are exhausted or you get what you want.” The story also appears in Stories of the Arabs, by Muhammad Ahmad Jad al-Mawla and his colleagues, Cairo, 1948, vol. 3, pp. 98–99. Hatim’s own verse is significant here: “They say to me: You have wasted your wealth, so be moderate / Yet without the very things they criticize, I would never have been a chief.”↩︎

Two concrete examples illustrate this kind of ownership. 1. It is said that during the reign of King al-Nu‘man (583–605), Hajib ibn Zurara and Qays ibn Mas‘ud argued over which man among their peoples was the meanest. Al-Nu‘man sent someone to see and testify. When they reached the territory of Hajib ibn Zurara, they passed a man from his people, and Hajib said: “This is the meanest of my people.” The man was beside his water basin, watering his camels. See Mahmud Shukri al-Alusi, Reaching the Goal, Cairo, 1923, vol. 1, p. 286. Note the phrase “his basin”: the water source was therefore this man’s property. The rest of the story says that he refused to give these people water from “his basin” even after learning that their tribal chief Hajib ibn Zurara was among them, although the story says that they had “entered Hajib’s territory.” 2. In a story about Qays ibn al-Khatim, who died in 2 AH, when he set out to avenge the killers of his father and grandfather, he went to his water-drawing camel while it was irrigating his palm grove. A nadih is the camel used to turn the waterwheel. See al-Aghani, vol. 3, p. 3. Here Qays ibn al-Khatim clearly owns a garden, along with a well or irrigation channel from which he waters it using his own waterwheel driven by his camel.↩︎

The person meant here is al-Muttalib ibn Abd Manaf, father of Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet’s grandfather. The alliance began when Banu Bakr ibn Abd Manat ibn Kinana planned during al-Muttalib’s time to drive Quraysh out of the Sanctuary and fight them. Commercial contacts brought many things into pre-Islamic society: craft skills, practical knowledge of agriculture and technical tools, a variety of ideas and beliefs, and many urban customs. Tribal leaders and major Qurayshi merchants also adopted valuable household goods. Through their trading journeys, tribal chiefs and leading Qurayshi caravan merchants learned about political events in the outside world and about the social problems facing neighboring peoples. These problems accompanied the decline caused by the two empires exhausting themselves in struggles over the Mediterranean lands and the main parts of the Arabian Peninsula, especially Yemen and the Hijaz.↩︎
